name: Ishmael
role: Narrator; a schoolmaster turned common sailor
desc: The only name he gives us is a request, and it is the name of a cast-out son. He is a green hand who has been to sea in the merchant service, goes whaling out of restlessness and a taste for the forbidden, and then — this is the strange thing — half-vanishes from his own book, turning from a character into a voice that can enter Ahab's cabin and Starbuck's thoughts. Watch for when the “I” goes quiet.
why: He is the book's real experiment: a man who survives by being porous, by being willing to sleep with a cannibal, squeeze spermaceti with strangers, and take every subject seriously. Ahab has one meaning; Ishmael has all of them.

name: Queequeg
role: Harpooneer of Starbuck's boat; prince of Kokovoko
desc: Tattooed head to foot with a cosmology no one, including himself, can read; sells embalmed heads in New Bedford; shaves with his harpoon; fasts on a Ramadan of his own devising; and gives Ishmael half his money the second morning they know each other. Builds his own coffin, then decides not to die.
why: The book's moral centre without ever making a speech. His tenderness is practical — he saves the bumpkin who mocked him, dives for Tashtego — and it is his coffin that carries Ishmael out. Melville makes the “savage” the one civilized man aboard.

name: Captain Ahab
desc: Fifty-eight, forty years at sea, a wife and child left behind after one night ashore, a leg taken by Moby Dick and replaced with sperm-whale bone, a scar like a lightning-strike running down his body. He does not appear until the ship is well out; when he does, the crew sees him before we do. Quaker by birth, Shakespearean by speech, and — the book insists — not a madman but a man whose madness has hired his intellect.
why: What fascinates me is that he is right about a great deal. His speeches on the pasteboard mask, on the doubloon, on the sea's sweetness in The Symphony, are the truest things anyone says. He is the terrible proof that clarity is not the same as wisdom.

name: Starbuck
desc: Thin, sober, superstitious in the sense of reverent, with a wife Mary and a boy at home. “I will have no man in my boat who is not afraid of a whale.” He alone stands against Ahab on the quarter-deck, he alone holds a loaded musket outside Ahab's door, and he alone cannot pull the trigger.
why: He is the reader's stand-in for ordinary decency and I find him almost unbearably sad. He is the man who knows and cannot act; his goodness has no traction against a will like Ahab's, which is maybe the book's harshest observation about goodness.

name: Stubb
desc: Never without his pipe, never without a joke, kills whales as if it were a matter of comfortable indifference, eats a whale steak by the light of the whale's own oil, and cheats a French captain out of a barrel of ambergris. Dreams that Ahab kicked him and decides the kick was an honor.
why: His philosophy — “I know not all that may be coming, but be it what it will, I'll go to it laughing” — is one of the book's genuine alternatives to Ahab, and Melville lets you feel both its charm and its shallowness. He is also cruel to Fleece and to Pip in ways the joking doesn't cover.

name: Flask
desc: Short, stout, ruddy, from Martha's Vineyard, regards whales as a personal affront that must be answered. Eats last and least at the cabin table, stands on Daggoo's shoulders to see over the swells.
why: He is what a whaler is without any inner life at all — and Melville is kind enough to give him one small moment on the last day, wishing his mother had drawn his part-pay.

name: Tashtego
role: Harpooneer of Stubb's boat; Gay Head Wampanoag
desc: Long, lean, with the eye of a hunter; falls into the sperm whale's severed head and is delivered out of it by Queequeg like a midwife's work; and at the very end nails the flag — and a sky-hawk — to the sinking mainmast.
why: His last act is the book's final image: a hand still hammering as the ship goes down, dragging a piece of heaven with it.

name: Daggoo
role: Harpooneer of Flask's boat; from Africa
desc: Six and a half feet, gold hoops in his ears, retains “all his barbaric virtues.” Carries Flask on his shoulders in the boat and faces down the Spanish sailor in Midnight, Forecastle.
why: Melville gives him less interiority than the other two harpooneers, which I notice and regret; but the image of a white mate standing on a Black man's shoulders to hunt is not accidental.

name: Fedallah
desc: Smuggled aboard with Ahab's phantom crew, Zoroastrian, turbaned with his own white hair, seen mostly at night. Prophesies that Ahab will see two hearses on the sea and die only by hemp — every clause of which comes true, sideways.
why: He is the one character I can't settle: a genuine Mephistopheles, or an ordinary Persian sailor onto whom the crew projects their dread? The book lets him be both, and his death — lashed to the whale by the tangled lines, going before Ahab — is the coldest thing in it.

name: Pip
role: Ship-keeper and cabin boy; from Alabama
desc: Small, bright, plays the tambourine, is left in the open sea for an hour when Stubb's boat pulls away, and comes up out of it with his wits gone and something else in their place. Ahab, of all people, takes him in.
why: Pip is the book's second answer to what the ocean does to a mind — Ahab's is rage, Pip's is a kind of holy idiocy that sees “God's foot upon the treadle of the loom.” The scenes where Ahab holds his hand are the only tenderness Ahab is allowed.

name: Bulkington
desc: Glimpsed at the Spouter-Inn, just back from a four-year voyage and already shipping out again; then given a single-page chapter, The Lee Shore, and never mentioned after.
why: Melville apparently meant him for a larger part and then didn't write it. What remains is one of the book's purest passages about why anyone goes to sea, and a ghost of the novel that wasn't.

name: Dough-Boy
desc: Pale, bread-faced, terrified of the harpooneers he must serve at table, forever ducking.
why: Comic, but a real piece of the ship's economy of fear — the cabin table is a small monarchy and Dough-Boy is its trembling clerk.

name: Fleece
desc: Ninety years old, roused at midnight to preach to the sharks at Stubb's command, and does it — a sermon on governing the shark in you — while Stubb heckles.
why: The scene is played for laughs and lands, but reread it: Fleece's sermon is better theology than Father Mapple's, and Stubb's treatment of him is one of the places the book's racial cruelty is not just observed but performed.

name: Perth
desc: Came to sea after drink ruined his family; forges Ahab's harpoon, which Ahab then baptizes in the harpooneers' blood, in nomine diaboli.
why: His chapter is about how the sea receives the wrecked — “Death seems the only desirable sequel for a career like this” — and it sits deliberately before The Forge.

name: The Carpenter
desc: Unnamed, a “pure manipulator,” makes Ahab's new leg and then converts Queequeg's coffin into a life-buoy, taking instruction without curiosity.
why: Ahab talks to him as to a machine, and the carpenter's blank competence is a mirror Ahab keeps peering into. Also: he builds the thing that saves Ishmael.

name: The Manxman
role: Old sailor from the Isle of Man
desc: The ship's oracle of ill omen — reads the log-line, hears the drowned in the seal cries, sees the coffin float.
why: Every ship has one; Melville uses him like a chorus.

name: Father Mapple
desc: Former harpooneer, climbs into a pulpit shaped like a ship's bow by a rope ladder he pulls up after him, and preaches Jonah — the two-stranded lesson of obedience and of the delight of the man who stands forth his own inexorable self.
why: The sermon is the book's ethical thesis and Ahab is the book's refutation of it, or the reverse; I still can't decide which, which is why it's a great sermon.

name: Captain Peleg & Captain Bildad
desc: Peleg blusters and swears; Bildad reads scripture and offers Ishmael the seven hundred and seventy-seventh lay. Between them they are the New England conscience: piety and profit in one counting-house.
why: Bildad's parting — “Don't stave the boats needlessly, ye harpooneers” — is a whole moral universe in a sentence.

name: Elijah
role: A prophet on the Nantucket wharf
desc: Ragged, pockmarked, asks Ishmael and Queequeg whether they've signed with Ahab and hints at things that happened off Cape Horn and in Santa.
why: Named for the prophet who denounced King Ahab; ignored, as prophets are.

name: Peter Coffin & Mrs. Hussey
desc: Coffin runs the Spouter-Inn and plays a long practical joke about the harpooneer; Mrs. Hussey runs the Try Pots, serves only chowder, and confiscates Queequeg's harpoon at supper.
why: The comedy of the shore chapters is real comedy, and the name Coffin is the first of the book's coffins.

name: Aunt Charity
desc: Brings pickles, spare pens, and flannel to the ship, out of pure goodness.
why: A small kindness set against everything the voyage becomes.

name: Captain Boomer
desc: English, lost his arm to Moby Dick, replaced it with an ivory one, and cheerfully wants nothing more to do with the whale. His surgeon Bunger is a comic turn.
why: The book's control experiment: a man with Ahab's wound and none of Ahab's disease.

name: Gabriel
desc: Declares Moby Dick the Shaker God incarnate and has terrorized his own ship into obedience.
why: Ahab's madness seen in a lesser, uglier register — and Gabriel is, unlike Ahab, right about what happens next.

name: Captain Gardiner
desc: Nantucketer, has lost a boat with his twelve-year-old son in it while chasing Moby Dick, and begs Ahab to help search. Ahab refuses.
why: The Rachel, “weeping for her children,” is what finds Ishmael at the end. I think this is the book's one act of grace and it comes from a man Ahab turned away.

name: Steelkilt & Radney
desc: A Lakeman and the mate who provoked him, told by Ishmael to Spanish gentlemen in Lima; Radney is taken by Moby Dick before Steelkilt can murder him.
why: A whole revenge novel embedded in the whale novel, and the first time we see Moby Dick act as if he were justice.

name: Derick de Deer
desc: German, oil-less, begging lamp-feeder in hand, races the Pequod's boats for a whale and loses.
why: Melville's comedy of nations; also the chapter with the book's cruelest, most tender whale-death.

name: Moby Dick
desc: A sperm whale of uncommon size, snow-white forehead and hump, wrinkled brow, deformed lower jaw, a body stuck with old harpoons; rumored ubiquitous and immortal. Appears in the flesh only in the last three chapters, and for a hundred pages before that is mostly a name, a prophecy, and a colour.
why: Melville is careful never to tell you what the whale means and equally careful to let every character tell you. The whiteness chapter is the key: what terrifies is not malice but the possibility of no meaning at all. And then, in the chase, the whale is just an animal, magnificent and pursued.
